title: Conditionals
summary: Branch your program's behavior with if / elif / else, and understand truthiness.

checkpoints.title: if / elif / else
checkpoints.content: `if condition:` runs its indented block only when the condition is true. `elif` checks another condition if the first was false, and `else` catches everything else. Python checks them top to bottom and stops at the first match.
checkpoints.explanation: Indentation is what defines the block in Python — there are no curly braces, so consistent indentation is required, not just style.

hints.H0: Only one branch of an if/elif/else chain ever runs.
hints.H1: Python stops checking as soon as one condition matches.
hints.H2: else always runs if nothing above it matched.

checkpoints.title: Predict a branch
checkpoints.content: `score = 72`, then `if score >= 90: print("A")`, `elif score >= 80: print("B")`, `elif score >= 70: print("C")`, `else: print("F")` — which one prints?

options.explanation: 72 fails the >= 90 and >= 80 checks, but passes >= 70, so that branch runs and Python stops there.
72 is not >= 80, so the B branch is skipped.
else only runs if every condition above it was false — but score >= 70 is true, so else never gets checked.

checkpoints.explanation: Python evaluates elif conditions in order and stops at the first true one — 72 first fails >= 90 and >= 80, then matches >= 70.

hints.H0: Check each condition from top to bottom, in order.
hints.H1: 72 is not >= 90 or >= 80, but it is >= 70.
hints.H2: The C branch runs, and nothing after it is checked.

checkpoints.title: Write a condition
checkpoints.content: Write the `if` line (including the colon) that only runs when the variable `temperature` is above 100.
checkpoints.explanation: "Above" means strictly greater than, so `>` is correct — `>=` would also match exactly 100.

hints.H0: "Above" a value means strictly more than it, not equal to it.
hints.H1: Don't forget the colon at the end of the line.

checkpoints.title: Predict truthiness

options.text: The block is skipped — an empty list is falsy.
options.explanation: Empty collections (lists, strings, dicts, sets) are falsy in Python; only a non-empty one is truthy.

options.text: The block runs — any list is truthy.
options.explanation: It's the contents that matter, not the type — an empty list is falsy specifically because it has no elements.

options.text: It raises a TypeError because a list isn't a boolean.
options.explanation: Python doesn't require an actual boolean here — every value has a truthiness, lists included.

checkpoints.explanation: Python treats empty containers (`[]`, `""`, `{}`, `set()`) as falsy, and non-empty ones as truthy — no explicit length check needed.

hints.H0: This is about the list being empty, not about lists in general.
hints.H1: Empty collections of any kind are falsy in Python.
hints.H2: if items: is skipped when items is [].
